🚀 Excited to share our open-source Malware Analysis & Memory Forensics Dataset on Hugging Face!

Memory forensics provides a critical window into detecting evasive, fileless, and in-memory ransomware attacks, but traditional analysis workflows have historically relied on manual, time-intensive inspection.

To support the security and ML communities with reproducible, scalable detection workflows, I have open-sourced a full end-to-end memory forensics dataset, curated detection rules, and automated extraction pipelines.

This work was conducted under the mentorship and guidance of Prof. Sonika Malik, whose direction was instrumental in shaping the methodology and translating raw forensic dumps into a structured, ML-ready benchmark.

📊 Dataset Highlights
18 Raw Memory Dumps: 6 benign baseline environments + 12 active ransomware captures (~4.5 GB each, ~470 GB raw data total)

Target Ransomware Families: WannaCry, Cerber, GandCrab, Jigsaw, TeslaCrypt, ViraLock, BlueHowl, Annabelle, and Vipasna

18 Extracted ELF Binaries: Benign and malicious binary samples extracted directly from VM states

Pre-extracted Volatility Scans: Forensic artifact outputs from malfind, pslist, psscan, pstree, psxview, vadinfo, vadwalk, yarascan, and memmap

100+ Curated YARA Rules: Targeted detection covering packers, cryptographic routines, exploit kits, and ransomware family attribution

Automation & Analysis Artifacts: Automated Volatility orchestration scripts, feature engineering pipelines, and structured scan outputs (~33 GB)

🔗 Access the Dataset & Code
Analysis Dataset: Hugging Face Dataset

Raw Dumps & Scans: Hugging Face Storage Bucket

Pipeline & Tools: GitHub Repository

Bash

# Download analysis dataset via HF CLI
hf download Vedaang/malware_analysis

# Sync raw ransomware memory dumps
hf sync hf://buckets/Vedaang/malware-analysis-data/Ransomware_Analysis ./ransomware
A special thanks to Prof. Sonika Malik for her continuous mentorship throughout this project, as well as the open-source Volatility and YARA developer communities whose tools power this analysis.

Feel free to explore the repository, clone the data buckets, and use the pipeline in your security and ML workflows!

𝗪𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗔𝗜 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗯𝘆 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘅 𝟳𝟱% & 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗯𝘆 𝟮𝟱% 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗵𝗶𝘁 𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆. 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲'𝘀 𝗵𝗼𝘄.

Recently, while designing an agentic system to automate business process audits for a client, we ran into something every team building agentic systems eventually faces: 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗯𝗹𝗼𝗮𝘁 & 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀.

The more agents, tools, and steps involved, the more tokens the system quietly burns — and if the architecture isn’t thought through, cost and latency creep up fast.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲: An audit automation system to check whether business policies & FCPA laws are being followed diligently across different geographies — validating evidence like emails, contracts, approval screenshots, and bills etc. against validation checklist (avg. 30 checks for each business function).

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗽: Three agents — Policy Assessment, Evidence Testing, and an Audit Assistant co-pilot — built on Google ADK.

A few 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀 helped us bring 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗯𝘆 𝟳𝟬-𝟳𝟱% 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘂𝗽 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆

𝟭. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗹𝗼𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 (𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀) - Rather than loading entire policies into the agent's context, we structured them as skills.md files — a summary layer, with detailed sections pulled in only when relevant to the check at hand. This alone 𝗰𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗯𝘆 𝟮𝟱-𝟯𝟱% 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗯𝘆 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟮𝟬%.

𝟮. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 – 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗴𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 - With multiple steps in the workflow — skill use, tool use — every model call was cache-enabled. We saw 𝗰𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗶𝘁 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝟳𝟬-𝟴𝟱%, billed at a fraction of base token cost. The effect was significant: 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗱𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝗹𝘆 $𝟭.𝟲𝟱 𝘁𝗼 $𝟬.𝟱𝟬. (Worth noting — cache writes have their own cost, so the savings only hold if reads outpace writes.)

𝟯. 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗹, 𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝘂𝗯-𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝘀𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 - Rather than one agent working through all 30 checklist items in sequence — carrying accumulated c
